Groundwork for Neural Network-Based Speciﬁc
Emitter Identiﬁcation Authentication for IoT
Jason M. McGinthy, Student Member, IEEE, Lauren J. Wong, and Alan J. Michaels, Senior Member, IEEE
Abstract—Trust is a prominent concern with the continued
expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT). As new devices enter
the market, device security must be a design pillar. In order to
trust these devices, they must be identiﬁable and authenticated
before they begin transmitting possible sensitive information, and
given the vast number of IoT devices in the future, it may
prove difﬁcult to properly trust and authenticate these authorized
devices on networks with current methods. Machine learning
neural networks have the ability to uniquely identify transmitters
based on their physical waveform characteristics which could be
used to identify and authenticate IoT nodes in large networks
with little impact to latency, providing an extra layer of security
and trust. This paper presents the groundwork for performing
neural network-based speciﬁc emitter identiﬁcation (SEI) on
resource constrained IoT devices using only raw in-phase and
quadrature (IQ) streams, with protocols to secure IoT networks.
As proof of concept, an existing neural network-based SEI
algorithm is executed on both a resource-rich and a more
resource-constrained device with low latency, demonstrating the
feasibility of using such algorithms on IoT devices now and in
the future.
Index Terms—Internet of Things, Security, Authentication,
Neural Networks, Speciﬁc Emitter Identiﬁcation, RF Fingerprint-
ing
I. INTRODUCTION
The Internet of Things (IoT) is becoming more common-
place in our everyday lives and experts expect the number
of these devices to grow past 50 billion by the year 2020
[1]. The IoT aims to improve many aspects of our lives
through efﬁciency. For example, smart homes, smart vehicles,
and smart city infrastructures are being designed to reduce
energy costs by incorporating numerous sensors and devices
that can automatically change their behavior to better react
to our behavioral patterns [2]. Further, the healthcare industry
is turning to IoT-based solutions for in-home and personal
care [3], and industrial IoT (IIoT) networks are being utilized
to improve product manufacturing, production, and storage.
These IoT networks are typically well-deﬁned and hierarchical
in nature [4], and are conﬁgured for speciﬁc purposes, such as
a factory ﬂoor layout for manufacturing [5]. Such general net-
work topologies help reduce many unknown factors of wireless
sensor networks (WSNs) by limiting the size, mobility, and
communication routing of IoT devices. However, security
requirements for these networks is not diminished. Conversely,

as the IoT continues to grow, security will become a bigger
concern as these devices will have access to and provide
personal and/or private information about people, vehicles, and
critical structures and systems.
The size and ﬂexibility of the IoT brings other unique
security concerns even when traditional security schemes are
properly implemented. For example, the scalability of IoT
increases the possibility for remote device or data observation,
allowing an attacker to collect vast amounts of information to
help in reverse engineering of security protocols [6]. The use
of authentication techniques in such a network ensures that
only trusted devices are able to communicate on a network.
However, most authentication protocols currently used only
perform non-physical data inspection (i.e. data content, not
physical signal), similar to Data Encryption Standard (DES)
[7], Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA) [8], WPA2 [9], or elliptic
curve cryptography (ECC) [10], harboring latent defects. More
speciﬁcally, they fail to authenticate the actual device which
can lead to possible device compromise or impersonation, as
all of the involved parameters can be observed, guessed, or
replicated [11]. As the number of small, poorly authenticated,
wireless IoT devices continues to grow, common network
attacks such as eavesdropping, man-in-the-middle (MITM),
denial of service (DoS), node impersonation, and battery
draining [12], [13], [14], will only become more prevalent, if
security continues to be neglected. Though, methods have been
developed and implemented to perform device authentication,
such as physically unclonable features (PUFs), recent work
has shown that the deterministic responses of PUFs can be
replicated [15]. Therefore, a method by which to authenticate
devices through non-deterministic and truly unclonable means
is imperative. Additionally, because re-deploying networks of
physical IoT devices with improved security systems is likely
cost prohibitive in response to latent security vulnerabilities,
more robust software-based device authentication techniques,
such as radio frequency (RF) ﬁngerprinting, which could be
incorporated into the IoT device’s layered defenses during
production and could be updated remotely, are needed.
In the IoT-realm, low-cost, mass produced devices are often
considerably resource-constrained. Consequently, our research
aims to pave the way for a low-cost, low-power, and low-
latency multi-factor authentication method utilizing neural
networks (NNs). More speciﬁcally, this work investigates
the feasibility of using NNs which cue on the minor, but
unique, perturbations of physical (PHY) layer characteristics
on the transmitted signals (RF ﬁngerprints), for multi-factor
authentication. When used in addition to other lightweight
security schemes, such a solution would provide a robust,

layered security approach appropriate for IoT devices [16].
To show feasibility, the use of NN-based SEI algorithms for
IoT node authentication is examined using a NN-based SEI
algorithm previously developed [17], [18]. NN-based authen-
tication usage protocols for various device and network types
are also discussed, and the approach given in [18] is executed
on both a resource-rich and more resource-constrained device.
The additional memory and computational costs associated
with the granularity of such NN-based SEI methods will be
examined in the context of the considered approach.
The results shown herein indicate that NN-based SEI al-
gorithms will need further reﬁning before implementation in
today’s large-scale systems, highlighting the challenges in
dealing with NNs in IoT [19]. However, there are numerous
beneﬁts to integrating NN-based authentication techniques
into the IoT. An approach like that in [18] is well-suited
to IoT networks because of the large variation amongst low-
cost, mass-produced nodes, caused by relaxed manufacturing
tolerances. Such variances result in a highly diverse set of
RF ﬁngerprints which are difﬁcult to impersonate based on
their analog nature [20]. Using NN-based techniques to help
identify and authenticate IoT using their RF ﬁngerprints is
particularly promising as such an approach reduces the need
for human oversight. More speciﬁcally, a NN approach to
device authentication can operate on the incoming raw IQ
data, eliminating the use of a priori-determined, expert-deﬁned
features often used. This makes the approach more ﬂexible
and robust because feature extraction techniques are often
only accurate over a limited parameter range, can be heavily
effected by channel conditions, and can be inconsistent. In
NN-based approaches, these effects can be far less severe, as
they can be trained for. Operating on the raw IQ data stream
can also lead to lower latency, as feature extraction can be
time consuming,[21], [18] and computation would be reduced
for transmitting devices because RF ﬁngerprints are implicit
in each transmission. As a result, NN-based SEI shows great
promise in the rapidly growing ﬁeld of IoT security and adds
a much needed layer of security to these devices.
The rest of this paper is organized as follows: In Section II,
recent works in the area of NN and other machine learning-
based SEI algorithms are described. Sections III and IV detail
current IoT security techniques and the IoT model used in
this work. In Section V, current SEI techniques are discussed.
Additionally, the NN-based SEI approach considered in this
work is also presented and described in detail in Section V,
including the NN design and algorithm performance.. NN-
based SEI is discussed in the context of IoT in Section VI,
and possible usage protocols are given. Section VII presents
and discusses the results of the considered NN-based SEI
algorithm’s performance on different classes of devices for
use in the IoT realm. Finally, directions for future work and
conclusions are provided in Sections VIII and IX.
II. RECENT WORK
While machine learning (ML) and NN techniques provide
the framework to eliminate the need for expert-deﬁned fea-
tures, recent works in ML and NN-based SEI have continued
to depend on these hand-crafted features. Most pertinent to
this work, in [22], RF ﬁngerprinting was used with deep
learning NNs in cognitive radio networks to identify emitters
using error signals (the difference between the received signal,
which contains emitter speciﬁc effects, and the ideal trans-
mitted signal), work by Patel et al. [23] created an RF-DNA
ﬁngerprint using statistical features (such as the variance and
kurtosis, of the instantaneous amplitude, frequency, and phase
of the received signal) which were matched to known emitters
using ensemble classiﬁers, and recent work by Chatterjee et al.
detailed RF-PUFs and their characteristics and used symbol-
based NNs for node authentication [15]. However, in both [22]
and [23], knowledge of the transmitted signal’s modulation
scheme or the transmitted signal itself is assumed, and the
approaches are unable to identify emitters unseen during
training [23]. Additionally, the work in [15] highlighted the
impacts of outside factors such as temperature on the approach,
indicating RF-PUFs are susceptible to environmental changes.
Other work of interest, include [24], [25] and [26]. In these
works, pre-deﬁned expert features were used as input to NN
or orther ML-based SEI algorithms, such as inﬁnite Gaus-
sian mixture models (IGMMs), to calculate device proximity,
perform session key establishment between nodes, distinguish
and authenticate physical devices, and detect anomalies at a
gateway-level.
III. SECURITY BACKGROUND
Many security practices focus primarily on information
security areas of concern: conﬁdentiality, integrity, and avail-
ability [27]. However, the IoT networks introduces new issues
with additional complexities to security, due to their size and
ﬂexibility, as well as the use of low-cost devices. Therefore,
device authentication is becoming an increasingly important
element of the multi-factor security system, in addition to
the current information security practices. Figure 1 highlights
the Transmission Control Protocol and the Internet Protocol
(TCP/IP) network stack and where the following security
and communications protocols mainly reside. While current
network security protocols such as Datagram Transport Layer

nor IPSec are lightweight enough to be executed on IoT de-

A. IoT Security
The communication and security schemes commonly used
in IoT systems, described below, are often based on traditional
security practices. While many of these security schemes
provide data security, they do not provide a reliable method
for performing device authentication. Additionally, many of
these techniques and security schemes require multiple trans-
missions between devices and additional computational efforts
from both devices to calculate the response to the challenge.
1) Bluetooth: Bluetooth is a short-range communication
protocol that aims to provide low-power links amongst con-
nected devices. Bluetooth relies on an initial pairing of devices
with a shared secret value, which may be observed by an
adversary, to allow a device to initially join a network.
Bluetooth security is based on a combination of device ID,
random number generator (RNG) value, personal identiﬁcation
number (PIN), and shared link key to perform authentication
and other security features [31]. However, Bluetooth only
veriﬁes device authentication based on these values. Therefore,
given the ability to watch the pairing process, attackers are
able to retrieve and replicate the necessary values, achieving
the synchronization necessary to spoof a device. Because
the actual user of the device is never authenticated, the
network is unable to distinguish one device from another, and
the possibility of an attacker gaining access to the network
remains. Successful spooﬁng and man-in-the-middle attacks
on Bluetooth devices have been achieved in the past due to
these vulnerabilities [32].
2) Zigbee: Zigbee [33] is a communication protocol stan-
dard that is based on the IEEE 802.15.4 wireless personal
area network (WPAN) standard [34]. These WPANs allow
for the manufacturing and operation of low-cost devices in
wireless networks, making this protocol ideal for many IoT
systems. Zigbee allows network administrators to broadcast
unencrypted network keys to all devices when adding new
devices to the network, creating a vulnerability for an attacker
to take advantage and attempt to perform device impersonation
or MITM attacks. Similar to Bluetooth, the Zigbee protocol
performs data encryption and message integrity checks, but
the protocol has no ability to perform actual unique device
authentication. Moreover, practical attacks against Zigbee have
been performed [35], [36], and a Python-based exploitation
tool, KillerBee, has been open-sourced [37]. Zigbee also is
based on a time-division multiple access (TDMA) carrier
sensing multiple access with collision avoidance (CSMA/CA)
protocol, which can be easily disrupted with timing attacks due
to the hidden node problem [38], to inexpensively implement
DDoS attacks.
3) Long Range Wide Area Network (LoRaWAN):
Lo-
RaWAN is a proprietary communication protocol designed
for low-cost, low-power devices [39]. LoRaWAN is similar
to the previous schemes in attempts to provide security to
IoT networks. LoRaWAN utilizes 128-bit cryptographic keys
for network formation and data encryption. It provides two
methods for devices to join a network: Over-the-Air Activation
(OTAA) and Activation by Personalization (ABP) [39]. In
[40], a vulnerability in the ABP procedure was exploited
through device physical tampering and allowed the security
keys to be compromised. Then, the attackers were able to
fully impersonate the compromised device and communicate
on the network undetected due to the inability of the network
to perform actual physical device authentication.
4) IEEE 802.11p: The IEEE 802.11p standard [41] is the
basis for inter-vehicular communication and between cars and
infrastructure at the PHY and MAC layers based on the normal
WiFi standard. The purpose of this standard is to provide very
fast communication capability due to the nature of vehicular
movement. The downside of this fast communication is the
lack of overall authentication, which must be handled at higher
levels. As more smart vehicles and infrastructure become
widespread, the use of this standard will grow, requiring fast
authentication of devices.
B. Multi-factor Authentication
Because many of the previously described protocols focus
on network formation and data security, true device identity is
still a major concern. Therefore, multi-factor authentication
(MFA) techniques must be utilized to increase trust and
security in IoT networks [14], [42]. MFA can generally be
achieved by performing at least two of the following methods:
what you possess (e.g. a physical token or ID card), what you
know (e.g. a password, PIN, or cryptographic key), or who you
are (e.g. unique physical characteristics) [42]. In many cases,
MFA is layered with the data encrypted through symmetric
cryptography [27], which requires both the transmitter and re-
ceiver to know the shared encryption key. However, for remote,
physically inaccessible nodes, it may not be possible to ensure
the device’s token will not be tampered with, making physical
possession the less preferred MFA method. For example, some
software packages require a physical key dongle plugged into
a computer to authorize use, but this method would not be
suitable for a remote device. Therefore, it is assumed that two-
factor authentication for resource-constrained IoT nodes will
be performed with a combination of knowledge (asymmetric
or symmetric cryptography) and physical characteristics. The
following sections highlight some of the current techniques
used to perform authentication based on these physical prop-
erties.
1) RF Fingerprinting: Similar to the use of biometrics,
such as retina scanners and ﬁngerprints, devices impart their
own unique analog modiﬁcations to signals, both on the
transmitter and receiver ends. Due to manufacturing process
variances, even the same devices can have minor differences

in their local oscillators and I-Q amplitude and phases imbal-

by using various signal analysis techniques to observe these

One caveat to this approach is the degradation of RF features
due to environmental factors such as temperature, pressure,
water density, other atmospheric conditions, and component
aging [44]. These factors may bound the actual performance
of some RF ﬁngerprinting methods. Therefore, special consid-
erations should be made in the design of a network, in order
to achieve desired performance. For instance, the number of
nodes in the network may be capped due to the additional
stored parameters for modeling different environmental cases.
2) Physically unclonable features (PUFs): PUFs are ideally
unique physical features embedded in the silicon components
of the chip during the manufacturing process [45]. A PUF
is typically a circuit that is designed to give a repeatable
response to a stimulus for use in a challenge-response scenario.
The actual manufacturing of this circuit introduces or exploits
minor imperfections in the manufacturing process producing a
unique signature to the actual response used for authentication,
much like an intentional RF ﬁngerprint. While PUFs are not a
secure communication protocol, they have been implemented
to provide physical device authentication. More speciﬁcally,
a challenge/response scheme is used to determine proper
authentication. In this practice, a device receives a challenge
command that invokes a response from the PUF based on that
speciﬁc command. Ideally, the correct response can only be
generated by the PUF and not replicated by any other process.
As previously discussed in other security applications, if the
contents of a device’s security scheme are compromised, an
attacker is able to impersonate a device. PUFs attempt to solve
this problem by providing an additional layer of authentication
for devices.
However, though PUFs attempt to be unclonable, research
has highlighted vulnerabilities with this technology. For ex-
ample, it has been shown that some ring oscillator-based
PUFs do not exhibit proper randomness for cryptographic
functions [46], and ML-based attacks have been successfully
been used against 65 nm CMOS Arbiter PUFs [47]. Despite
their shortcomings, researchers at MIT have done work with
PUFs for authentication, and have worked to protect them
against ML capabilities to learn the challenge/response pairs
(CRPs) [48].
IV. IOT MODEL
In order to determine the best use of a NN-based SEI
algorithm in IoT networks, assumptions for the network must
be deﬁned. The major components of the network are its
conﬁguration (size and topology) and its device makeup. These
main factors will help bound the parameters needed for proper
NN-based SEI in IoT.
A. Network Conﬁguration
Most IoT networks are heterogeneous in nature, due to
the different requirements of the systems involved. Therefore,
for certain network conﬁgurations, a proper device hierarchy

is implemented. This hierarchical design allows for easier
control of network trafﬁc because nodes are only able to
communicate with other authorized devices. Also, networks
with a priori knowledge of all devices allows an initial level
of trust amongst nodes, given the ability to whitelist allowed
connections. This hierarchical design can be used in many
different topologies, such as star-of-stars and both sparsely-
and densely-connected mesh networks, all of which will be
further discussed in the following sections.
1) Star-of-Stars: The star-of-stars (also known as hub-and-
spoke) network model, shown in Figure 2, is a very simple
design. It allows for many edge nodes (ENs) to be connected
to a single access point (AP), which is then directly connected
to the central controller (CC). The routing is straightforward
which eases initial implementation, but also causes inﬂexibility
due to the minimum number of routes. Further, this topology
can suffer when APs fail, unless sufﬁcient resiliency considera-
tions are made, such as conﬁguring a backup AP for all nodes.
However, this model is still ideal for very resource constrained
ENs that have limited storage capabilities for routing tables as
only the main AP and backup AP(s) would need to be stored.
2) Sparsely-Connected
Mesh:
The
sparsely-connected
mesh network is similar to the star-of-stars model in design,
but allows for additional routing through speciﬁed relay de-
vices. Although this adds more complexity to the routing,
there are still hierarchical elements that help with determining
known routes, and this added ﬂexibility can help in networks
prone to interference. Figure 3 shows an example of a sparsely-
connected mesh network.
3) Densely-Connected Mesh: Figure 4 depicts an example
of a densely-connected mesh network. Densely-connected
mesh networks build on the concept of the sparse network,
but allow for links between all devices within communication
range. This greatly increases the complexity of storing routing
information, but also provides the greatest amount of ﬂexibility
and resilience. As an added beneﬁt, this type of network
structure supports a self-healing capability. More speciﬁcally,
when a link fails, a new route can be quickly reconﬁgured,
minimizing downtime. Network monitoring also provides the
ability to achieve low latency, by periodically calculating the
fastest and most reliable routes and via wireless adaptations of
time-sensitive networking [49]. However, due to the increase in

B. Devices
1) Edge Device: The edge device is typically the most
variable type of device in an IoT network. They are the major
contributor to the heterogeneous nature of these networks.
They can range from extremely resource-constrained, battery-
powered or possibly energy-harvested sensors, actuators, or
controllers to more capable devices with constant power
supplies. As an example of a resource-constrained device, the
MSP430FR5994 processor has 256 KB non-volatile memory,
8 KB RAM, and a maximum clock rate of 16 MHz [50],
which severely limits an SEI implementation on this type of
edge node. Therefore, the need to understand the lower bounds
of these devices for SEI algorithms must be well understood.
Based on the possible network topologies described above,
it may be assumed that a resource-constrained edge node
would only need a very limited SEI implementation. For
example, in a star-of-stars network, due to the well-deﬁned
and small number of links amongst devices, an edge node
may only need to perform simple binary authentication; i.e.,
authentication decisions as to whether or not an incoming
transmission belongs to its designated AP. However, as the
networks grow more complex, the feasibility of SEI on the
outer edge nodes becomes questionable. Because edge nodes
only need to identify nearby neighbors that are common links
(APs), shrinking the required number of stored parameters
should help increase the feasibility of some SEI techniques
on less capable devices.
2) Access Point: An access point in an IoT network will
most likely be more capable than its edge nodes, and is
typically more resource-rich with clock rates ≥1 GHz, RAM
capacities of ≥256 MB, memory storage ≥1 GB, as well as
a constant power supply. One example of this type of device
is the Cisco wireless gateway for LoRaWAN, which boasts a
1.33 GHz processor, 1 GB of RAM, and 4 GB of ﬂash memory

[51]. AP devices may be required to identify upwards of 100
devices on their subnet or combination of subnets (if used as
a back-up). However, as more IoT gateways continue to hit
the market with speciﬁcations similar to the Cisco wireless
gateway, the realization of NN-based SEI implementation
on these devices becomes very feasible, without signiﬁcant

3) Central Controller: The central controller (CC) is usu-
ally the master device of the entire network. The CC may also
act as a repository for all of the device’s SEI parameters (prop-
erly safeguarded) that can then be securely transferred to new
devices to achieve a type of transfer learning for the network.
The CC can be a traditional desktop computer, a server farm
(cloud), or may be composed of application-speciﬁc graphics
processing units (GPUs), depending on application. Therefore,
power, processor, and memory constraints of CCs will not need
to impact the SEI design.
4) Other: As the IoT continues to grow, new device types
may play bigger roles. For example, relay-type or other hybrid
devices may be needed to improve network performance with-
out the use of an additional gateway in order to lower costs.
These devices may be more capable than current edge nodes,
but will likely not be as resource-rich as APs. Additionally,
these devices may have long dwell times before waking up to
performing an expensive operation, which will impact how SEI
may be performed through these devices. Due to the unknown
nature of these devices, NN-based SEI methods will need to
be ﬂexible to allow for implementation on future node/device
types.
V. SEI BACKGROUND
A. Traditional SEI Techniques
SEI, the act of matching a received signal to an emitter, has
been performed in various domains, including the IoT [52],
[15]. Early SEI techniques were used to determine the make
and model of automobile engines using audio emissions and
harmonics [53]. RF-based SEI techniques continue to be used
in both commercial [54] and military [55] contexts to help in
determining friend from foe. SEI or RF ﬁngerprinting is possi-
ble because of the unique and unintentional characteristics that
an emitter imparts onto each transmission, commonly caused
by hardware imperfections and manufacturing inconsistency,

known as it’s RF ﬁngerprint. Traditional SEI techniques utilize
expert-deﬁned features to capture these RF ﬁngerprints in
tandem with clustering algorithms used for classiﬁcation and
veriﬁcation [55].
Expert-deﬁned features are typically either extracted from
the transient or steady state portion of the received signal.
Features extracted from the transient portion of the received
signal often examine the time-domain, frequency-domain, or
phase-space [56]. For example, a popular frequency domain
feature is the power spectral density [57]. The types of features
extracted from the steady state signal vary widely including
cyclic features [58], preamble periodicity [59], and wavelet
based features [60].
The primary limitation of traditional SEI techniques is the
use of these expert-deﬁned features to characterize emitters of
interest. Expert-deﬁned features are often only accurate over
a limited parameter range, can be heavily effected by channel
conditions, and are reliant on accurate and consistent feature
measurement [55], [61]. Further, expert-deﬁned features only
examine certain aspects of the received signal, and therefore
the selection of features that characterize the emitters of
interest is critical and can be time consuming. The extraction
of features itself can also be extremely computationally expen-
sive. In particular, transient processing typically requires high-
speed over-sampling. Raw IQ based NN feature extraction
techniques offer the potential for ﬁngerprinting when critically
sampled, lowering the computational expense.
B. NN Approaches to SEI
More recent work in SEI makes use of ML and NN-based
techniques, but often continues to use expert-deﬁned features
as input to these algorithms, such as ensemble classiﬁers and
neural networks, at the classiﬁcation step [22], [23], [62].
While these approaches often yield good results, the continued
reliance on expert-deﬁned features means that the limitations
outlined above are still highly relevant. Furthermore, these
approaches are often only able to classify a known set of
transmitters, failing to identify unknown emitters, and in the
worst cases, labeling unknown transmitters as one of the
learned classes.
The subset of NN techniques considered in this paper are
convolutional NN (CNN)-based, and operate only using the
received data, in raw IQ format, as input to the algorithm, re-
lying on the CNN to objectively form a set of machine-learned
features that enable accurate decision of the emitter. Two such
approaches were developed in prior work [21], [18]. In the ﬁrst
approach, a CNN was trained to estimate the IQ imbalance of
the transmitter [17]. By comparing the estimated gain offset
to Gaussian distributions ﬁtted to histograms of the CNN
output, the estimated gain offset value could be used to identify
emitters. Additionally, numerous estimates can be aggregated
to produce more accurate results [18]. The second approach
used a method called supervised bootstrapping to allow the
CNN to learn emitter speciﬁc features from a known set of
emitters. These features were fed to the density-based spatial
clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN) clustering
algorithm for classiﬁcation/identiﬁcation. It was then shown

C. Considered Approach
In the following sections, we examine the use of NN-
based SEI algorithms for IoT node authentication using the
algorithm presented in [18] and shown in Figure 5 as proof
of concept. While the protocols described below generalize
to any NN-based SEI algorithm that utilize only raw IQ data
as input, the approach considered here has several beneﬁts
lending itself to implementation on IoT devices. First, the
approach is modulation agnostic, and it does not depend on
a pre-trained classiﬁer, and as a result, the approach has the
potential to identify spoofers as well as the ability to whitelist
new emitters in real-time. Second, because the approach uses
the inherent feature learning abilities of CNNs rather than
hand extracted features, the approach requires only 1024 raw
IQ samples, or approximately 2 bytes worth of received data
symbols [22], to identify a device. However, given more
data, results can be aggregated to produce more accurate
identiﬁcation results. Once the IQ imbalance of the emitter
has been estimated using the CNN, the identiﬁcation and/or
veriﬁcation step is a simple and computationally inexpensive
lookup. Finally, because IoT devices are often low-cost, it
is likely they will exhibit more severe hardware impairments
than high-end emitters, as previously discussed. Therefore, the
approach will likely be able to uniquely identify more devices.
As brieﬂy described above, the considered approach is
CNN-based, and uses only the received signal, in raw IQ
format, as input, which may be obtained using any blind
signal detector, such as those found in [63]. Additionally,
the algorithm operates without use of test signals, successive
iterations, demodulation, or statistical measures, as is often
required in traditional IQ imbalance estimation approaches.
The considered approach is like the approach proposed in [15]
in that both approaches identify emitters using IQ imbalance,
a feature of the received signal caused by hardware non-
idealities in the transmitter. More speciﬁcally, a CNN is used
to estimate the gain offset of the transmitter, α, which is then
compared to Gaussian distributions ﬁtted to histograms of the
CNN output to identify or verify emitters, the details of which
can be found in [18].
While the considered approach and that given in [15] both
identify emitters using their IQ imbalance, the considered
approach uses only the raw IQ samples as input to the CNN,

that can be placed in remote, not easily accessible locations.
Therefore, careful considerations must be made in the overall
design of NNs for use on IoT devices. For example, IoT de-
vices may be battery powered with minimal memory, limiting
the number of NN trainable parameters that can be stored.
Generally, current NN or other ML applications in IoT are
data-driven processes used to help improve overall conﬁdence
in and efﬁciency of existing systems, rather than as a com-
ponent of the network stack. While there has been work in
successfully implementing deep learning network processors
on IoT-like devices [65], they are currently limited to tasks
such as facial recognition due to restricted memory capacities
(≤1 MB). As ongoing research continues to improve storage
size [66] and overall IoT capabilities evolve, there will be
more opportunities to implement NN-based algorithms on
these devices.
The setup and usage of the a NN-based SEI algorithm on a
network of IoT devices is dependent upon a variety of factors,
including network conﬁguration and device/system constraints.
However, it may be assumed that all APs, relay nodes, and
CCs will be capable of identifying N whitelisted devices and
detecting unknown devices. Additionally, it should be noted
that N may change dynamically over time as new devices join
or leave the network.
As previously mentioned, edge nodes will typically be more
resource-constrained than APs, relay devices, or CCs. In star-
of-stars or sparsely-connected mesh networks, edge nodes will
only need to verify a single AP or relay device. However, in a
densely-connected mesh network, edge nodes may also need
to be able to identify N devices as well.
As resource constraints are of primary concern when de-
ploying a NN-based SEI algorithm on IoT devices, edge nodes
in particular, it should be noted that the algorithm could be
utilized in an IoT network in several ways. While running the
SEI algorithm continuously would be most secure, it would
also require the most power and memory and incur the most
latency. Therefore, this is likely to only be feasible on a
resource-rich device such as the AP or CC. A more likely
use case is to run such an SEI algorithm periodically or on a
triggered basis. This will be less secure, yet its frequency of
initiation may be considered according to the value of the data
being communicated. However, periodic or triggered SEI use
is far more power efﬁcient, and will incur far less latency in
resource constrained systems. In the most resource-constrained
systems (i.e. edge nodes), it may also be possible to rely on
other devices for veriﬁcation. This is clearly the least secure
solution, as the verifying device will be assumed to be a trusted
device at all times. However, this risk can be improved by
strengthening the timing and distance proﬁle of the verifying
node. This solution will also incur the most latency, requiring
the node to transmit to another device and await response.
Given these trade-offs, three possible protocols for using a NN-
based SEI algorithm in an IoT network are described below.
A. One-Way SEI
Given that it is currently improbable to perform SEI on
a resource-constrained edge node, for certain networks, the

an AP is unlikely to be compromised, reducing the need for

B. Mutual Authentication Through a Secondary Device
Another approach, allowing mutual authentication for edge
nodes, is to perform SEI on a secondary device that is
physically located near the edge device, as shown in Figure
9. This secondary device would have more capabilities than
the typical edge node, such as a Raspberry Pi Zero class
device compared to an MSP430 class device, and would
perform SEI on-demand (triggered or random) from a nearby
edge node. This method allows the edge node to perform
its normal operations while off-loading the computationally
expensive authentication to a nearby, trusted device. In order
to make it infeasible for an attacker to impersonate either
of the devices, the distance and/or timing constraint between
the edge node and secondary device will need to be well-
deﬁned. The beneﬁt of this approach is that the secondary
device needs no knowledge of the actual message because only
raw IQ samples are needed as input to the proposed NN-based
SEI algorithm. Therefore, the secondary device can simply
perform the algorithm on the available transmissions from the
AP. Additionally, depending on the network structure, a single
secondary device could perform SEI for a small number of
nearby edge nodes (≤5).

VII. IOT IMPLEMENTATION RESULTS
Once the gain offset of an emitter has been estimated, the
identiﬁcation of said emitter is simply a lookup. Therefore
the computational burden is in executing the CNN gain offset
estimator. Therefore, this section describes the performance
of gain offset estimation CNN portion of the considered
approach, implemented in Python using the Keras and Ten-
sorﬂow libraries [68], [69], on both a resource-rich quad-core
Intel CPU [70] and a more resource constrained Raspberry
Pi Zero [71]. The Raspberry Pi Zero is considered due to its
low-cost and its ability to still run the CNN in Python. This
device still may provide higher computing capabilities than
battery-powered IoT devices, but it allows the ability to begin
to bound the CNN performance in the IoT realm. Our goal
is to move towards smaller systems on chips (SoCs) or more
resource-constrained battery-powered devices as the CNN is
further pruned to work in such devices.
The CNN used in the considered approach and described in
Section V-C requires approximately 7.2 million multiplies and
an equivalent number of adds to execute one signal capture
containing 1024 samples. On a single thread of an Intel
Xeon CPU E5-1620 v4 @3.5GHz processor [70], this requires
440 microseconds to execute. This highlights the feasibility
of executing NN-based SEI algorithms on central controllers
or extremely resource-rich APs, with extremely low latency.
However, the vast majority of edge nodes will not have this
level of capability.
The same CNN model was also executed on a Raspberry
Pi Zero [71], representing a more resource-constrained, edge
node class of device, housing an ARM11 1 GHz processor
with 512 MB of RAM and a removable SD card for non-
volatile memory. On this class of device, the current evaluation
was focused on the point-to-point link for an edge device’s
ability to perform SEI as a binary classiﬁer (i.e., if the AP
sent the message or not). Figure
11 shows a histogram of
the execution runtimes of the model on the Pi. The mean
execution time was approximately 123 ms with a mode of
approximately 108 ms, indicating that this class of device
is capable of performing NN-based SEI, with some latency
incurred. However, it should be noted that authentication does
not need to be performed on every burst, as was previously
discussed in Section VI. Furthermore, the considered algo-
rithm was not optimized for execution on such a device, and
therefore could likely be altered to signiﬁcantly reduce latency,
as discussed below in Section VIII.
Given these results, it is clear that implementing the con-
sidered algorithm on the most resource-constrained devices,
such as an MSP430FR5994, is not currently possible, nor
is it likely to be possible in the near future. However, the
algorithm, as currently implemented, could be integrated into
an IoT network using one of the proposed protocols given
in VI. Moreover, as IoT device capabilities improve, these
results show the promise of using NN-based SEI algorithms,
such as the considered approach, in networks containing
approximately 100 nodes.
VIII. FUTURE WORK
Although results have shown the feasibility of using an
NN-based SEI algorithm in IoT networks using the described
implementation schemes, several areas have been highlighted
as areas of future work to both improve such an algorithm and
further test it’s performance, increasing compatibility with IoT
networks. These areas are further described below.
A. Implementation on Additional IoT Devices
The biggest factors for implementing a NN-based SEI algo-
rithm are the memory footprint and clock rate of the device,
therefore the designed NN must ﬁt within allowed memory
capacities and the algorithm must not add undue latency to
the network. This work has shown that currently implemented
NN-based SEI algorithms meets the speciﬁcations of many IoT
access points and gateways. This is a critical junction in an IoT
network due to the fact that these devices are more resource-
rich and need to communicate amongst many other devices.
As the NN-based SEI algorithm’s footprint is reduced and
edge node capabilities increase, there may soon be a common
ground to implement a lightweight, but effective, algorithm
onto some edge nodes to allow mutual authentication of de-
vices without the need for expensive asymmetric cryptographic
techniques.

B. Decreasing Memory Requirements
It is clear that one of the primary limitations of using NN-
based SEI approaches on IoT devices is memory constraints.
For example, the CNN model developed to perform IQ im-
balance estimation in [18] is far too large to be placed on an
edge node, and may even be too large to be kept on some AP
devices. Therefore, when developing NN-based SEI algorithms
for use in IoT networks, attention needs to be paid to either
signiﬁcantly reduce the size of existing NN models or to the
development of high performing, yet small NN models.
The easiest method to reduce the memory footprint existing
NN models would be to retrain using 32-bit or even 16-bit
ﬂoats, as opposed to 64-bit ﬂoats. Additionally, model pruning
techniques such as those found in [72] and [73] may also be an
effective method by which to reduce the size of NN models.
Training or retraining a NN while enforcing sparsity of the
trainable parameters using methods such as those found in [74]
and [75] is also a promising approach to reducing the size of
existing or new NNs. Finally, ongoing research investigating
the robustness of feed-forward classiﬁcation NNs, such as
multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) and CNNs, to weight errors
during training and testing has also shown that errors in the
mantissa LSB have minimal performance impacts [76]. This
result could be applied to further prune memory coefﬁcient
sizes.
C. Decreasing Latency
Another primary concern in utilizing NN-based SEI algo-
rithms in IoT networks is the latency incurred as a result
of running these algorithms. While latency can be controlled
by executing the SEI algorithm less often, during critical
communications only, the latency of currently implemented
algorithms could be decreased in several ways. For example,
the considered approach was implemented in Python, and
would see signiﬁcant speedups after porting into a more
efﬁcient language such as C. Additionally, the dependencies on
open-source toolboxes, Keras and Tensorﬂow [68], [69], which
may not be optimally implemented, could also be removed
to further optimize the implemented algorithm. Efﬁcient hard-
ware implementations of neural networks is also an active area
of research that could also be applied to both reduce latency
and power consumption [77].
D. Further Testing
While the considered approach showed success using sim-
ulated RF data [18], the approach needs to be tested using
real RF data to further validate the feasibility of using such
an approach in an IoT setting. Future work looks to collect
data from a custom PHY-layer [78] to highlight the agnostic

E. SEI Algorithm Improvement
There are many ways in which the NN-based SEI can
be improved, increasing the feasibility of implementing such
algorithms on IoT devices. To increase the number of emitters
the approach can identify, the neural network architecture
could be further altered and optimized to achieve more ac-
curate gain offset estimates, or the approach be extended to
include the estimation of additional hardware impairments.
However, it should be noted that improvements such as these
may necessitate the use of larger or additional networks,
requiring additional computation or memory at the IoT nodes.
IX. CONCLUSIONS
This paper has provided the basis for using a NN-based SEI
algorithm as an additional layer of IoT device and network
security. More speciﬁcally, the challenges of using NN-based
SEI algorithms in IoT networks have been discussed, as well
as design considerations and existing algorithm improvements
to make using such algorithms feasible. This work has shown
that an existing NN-based SEI algorithm can be integrated into
systems as a device authentication technique, allowing multi-
factor authentication in IoT without human-device interaction,
with minimal latency on AP and CC class devices, as well as
on edge node class devices, when used on an ad-hoc basis.

Abstract  
Radio frequency (RF) fingerprinting leverages hardware-induced signal imperfections to uniquely 
identify devices, but conventional supervised deep learning methods degrade sharply under realistic 
conditions, including few-shot labeled data, open-set environments, channel distortions, temporal 
drift, modulation diversity, and dynamic operational settings, challenges prevalent in large-scale 
IoT, UAV swarms, and tactical networks. This work introduces RF-SSL, a semi-supervised 
framework designed for robust few-shot device identification and zero-shot anomaly detection amid 
extreme data scarcity and diverse RF impairments. RF-SSL integrates domain-informed 
augmentation (DIA) simulating channel effects, hardware imperfections, operational variations, and 
invariance-preserving transforms. It combines multi-task and contrastive self-supervised pretraining 
on unlabeled RF signals with shallow-to-medium CNN fine-tuning, with hyperparameters optimized 
for contrastive temperature (τ ≈ 0.1) and learning rate (1×10⁻³). Evaluation spans few-shot accuracy 
(1–20 shots), zero-shot anomaly AUC, and robustness to SNR, channel models, temporal drift, 
unseen modulations, convergence speed, and ablation studies. RF-SSL uniquely unifies physics-
informed, multi-category augmentation with multi-task contrastive pretraining, providing systematic, 
multi-dimensional benchmarking under simultaneous data scarcity, drift, and modulation shifts. 
Results show ~3× faster convergence, 15–40% improved robustness under impairments and drift, 
and better preservation of performance on unseen modulations (few-shot accuracy up to 0.95, 
anomaly AUC ~0.88). Ablations confirm DIA and contrastive pretraining as principal contributors, 
while shallow CNNs optimize speed, accuracy, and robustness. Overall, domain-informed semi-
supervised learning significantly enhances data efficiency, temporal stability, and generalization in 
RF fingerprinting, though absolute performance remains constrained in extreme impairment 
scenarios.

INTRODUCTION  
The IoT Security Landscape: Expanding 
Attack Surface at the Physical Layer  
 
The Internet of things (IoT) paradigm heralds an 
era of pervasive connectivity, with projections 
exceeding 75 billion connected devices by 2025 
[1]. This unprecedented scale introduces a 
massive, heterogeneous attack surface where 
traditional network and cryptographic security 
mechanisms are increasingly strained. While 
protocols like TLS and cryptographic keying 
provide data confidentiality and integrity at 
higher layers, they often prove computationally 
prohibitive 
for 
resource-constrained 
IoT 
endpoints or fail to address inherent physical-
layer vulnerabilities. The wireless medium itself 
becomes a critical threat vector, exposing 
systems to low-cost, scalable attacks such as 
device spoofing, rogue access point insertion, 
denial-of-service jamming, and signal replay 
[2].  
RF Fingerprinting as a Hardware-intrinsic 
Authentication Mechanism  
 
Radio frequency fingerprinting (RFF) emerges 
as a potent physical-layer security mechanism 
that exploits unavoidable, minute hardware 
imperfections 
introduced 
during 
the 
manufacturing process of wireless transmitters. 
These imperfections, manifesting as unique 
combinations of phase noise, I/Q imbalance, 
power amplifier non-linearity, and clock skew, 
imprint a persistent, device-specific signature 
onto every emitted RF signal, often termed a 
―hardware fingerprint‖ [3]. Unlike software-
based identifiers (e.g., MAC addresses), which 
can be trivially cloned, this hardware signature 
is exceedingly difficult to forge, offering a 
robust basis for device authentication. The 
classical RFF pipeline involves extracting 
distinguishing 
features, 
either 
via 
signal 
processing techniques (e.g., spectral features, 
transient analysis) or learned representations

The Brittleness of Supervised Learning: 
Challenges with Unseen Devices, 
Environmental Dynamics, and Data Scarcity 
 
The advent of deep learning has significantly 
advanced RFF, with convolutional and recurrent 
neural networks achieving high accuracy in 
controlled, closed-set identification tasks [5]. 
However, these supervised approaches exhibit 
profound brittleness when deployed in real-
world, 
dynamic 
IoT 
environments. 
Their 
performance is contingent on three critical and 
often unrealistic assumptions: a static universe 
of known devices, stationary environmental 
conditions, and the availability of abundant, 
meticulously labeled training data. First, a 
model trained on a fixed set of devices is 
inherently incapable of identifying unseen or 
newly deployed IoT nodes, categorizing them 
incorrectly among known classes, a fundamental 
limitation 
of 
the 
closed-set 
classification 
paradigm. Second, RF fingerprints are not static; 
they are modulated by dynamic channel effects 
(multipath fading, Doppler shift), temporal 
hardware drift (due to ageing or temperature), 
and varying signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) [6]. 
 
The Promise of Self-supervised 
Representation Learning  
 
Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) presents a 
transformative paradigm to overcome the 
fundamental limitations of supervised RFF. By 
learning generalizable representations from 
unlabeled data, SSL bypasses the need for 
exhaustive labeling. The core principle involves 
designing pretext tasks that force a model to 
learn meaningful, invariant features of the data 
without human annotation [7]. For RF signals, a 
well-designed pretext task, such as contrastive 
learning where the model must identify I/Q 
segments from the same device under different 
augmentations (e.g., simulated channel effects, 
noise), can teach the model to disentangle the 
invariant hardware signature from nuisance 
signal variations [8], [9].

and NLP (Foundational Concepts)

learning 
(SSL) 
has

data. 
Foundational 
pretext 
tasks 
include

learns by contrasting augmented views of the

a model pre-trained with a well-designed 
surrogate task produces representations that

The SSL‘s potential is established in other

security 
remains 
nascent. 
Preliminary

physics. This overlooks the critical need for 
domain-informed augmentations that accurately 
simulate RF-specific impairments to learn truly 
robust and invariant features. Furthermore, 
existing 
works 
typically 
address 
either

SSL framework that simultaneously enables 
data-efficient

fingerprinting

The proposed RF-SSL framework operates in 
two distinct stages, designed to decouple

from

pre-training phase that consumes a large corpus 
of unlabeled I/Q data Xu from a diverse 
population of IoT transmitters. The objective is 
to learn a universal, robust feature encoder Eψ 
via a contrastive pretext task. Stage 2 leverages 
the frozen or lightly fine-tuned pre-trained 
encoder for downstream tasks: Few-Shot Device 
Identification or Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection.

Datasets  
 
To ensure rigorous and generalizable evaluation, 
we employ two publicly available RF datasets. 
The primary dataset is the ORACLE dataset of 
ADS-B signals from 1000+ aircraft transponders 
[14]. It provides a large-scale, real-world 
benchmark with significant device diversity and 
captures inherent hardware variations. To 
validate cross-protocol performance, we also 
utilize the LORA dataset [18], containing 
signals 
from 
60 
LoRa-enabled 
devices, 
representing a common IoT protocol. This dual-
dataset approach allows us to assess our 
framework's 
robustness 
across 
different 
modulation schemes (ASK for ADS-B vs. CSS 
for LoRa) and application domains, ensuring 
conclusions are not artefact-specific.  
 
Comparison Baselines  
 
We establish a comprehensive suite of baselines 
for fair comparison:  
Supervised: A standard 1D-CNN architecture, 
serving as the upper-bound performance when 
trained with full labels [10].  
Semi-Supervised/Transfer Learning: A model 
pre-trained in a supervised manner on a large, 
labeled subset of devices and fine-tuned on the 
target set (the standard transfer approach). 
Unsupervised Anomaly Detection: A deep 
Autoencoder (AE) trained to reconstruct normal 
signals, 
with 
anomaly 
scores 
based 
on

SSL Baseline: A SimCLR-style model [7] pre-
trained 
using 
naive 
image-inspired

DISCUSSION  
 
The narrow 10-shot performance peak of RF-
SSL (+0.009 improvement) confirms prior 
findings that consistency-based semi-supervised 
learning (SSL) is effective only when minimal 
labeled anchors exist to reliably propagate 
pseudo-labels [19], [20]. In 5- and 20-shot 
regimes, noisy pseudo-labels and overfitting of 
consistency constraints induce negative transfer, 
consistent with challenges reported for purely 
consistency-driven SSL in RF fingerprinting 
[21]. 
Hybrid 
pipelines 
combining 
self-
supervised 
pretraining 
and 
adversarial 
augmentation exploit unlabeled RF corpora and 
hardware impairments more effectively [22], 
[23]. The ~3× convergence speedup (Fig. 1(d)) 
is significant for edge-based online adaptation in 
dynamic spectrum or IoT/UAV contexts, where 
energy and latency constraints are critical [24].  
Data-efficiency 
trends 
(Fig. 
1(e)) 
indicate RF-SSL degrades gracefully with 
decreasing shots but rarely surpasses supervised 
baselines, highlighting the limits of consistency 
regularization 
under 
extreme 
few-shot 
constraints. 
Metric-based 
meta-learning 
or 
contrastive self-supervised approaches that 
explicitly model inter-emitter similarity remain 
more effective [25], [26]. RF-SSL consistently 
outperforms supervised CNNs across ROC, 
AUC, AP, and FPR@95% recall, constructing 
robust decision boundaries under open-set 
anomaly conditions (Fig. 1(a)–1(f)) [19], [20]. 
AUC and AP increase with anomalies, reflecting 
semi-supervised 
refinement 
of 
legitimate 
fingerprint manifolds, though absolute values 
(0.65–0.82) reveal ongoing zero-shot challenges 
under 
noise, 
channel 
impairments, 
and 
sophisticated spoofing [21]–[24]. Low, stable 
FPR at high recall is crucial for resource-limited 
IoT, UAV, and tactical deployments [25].  
RF-SSL mitigates sensitivity to diverse 
impairments—including 
noise, 
multipath, 
phase/frequency offsets, I/Q mismatch, jitter, 
drift, and modulation changes—by enforcing 
prediction consistency across perturbed views, 
preserving discriminative hardware signatures 
more effectively than supervised baselines [19], 
[20]. Temporal drift studies confirm near-flat 
accuracy over a year despite ageing, thermal 
cycling, and voltage fluctuations, whereas 
supervised models degrade rapidly without 
recalibration 
[21], 
[22]. 
Modulation 
generalization is also superior: RF-SSL retains 
performance across BPSK, QPSK, 16QAM, and 
GFSK by learning hardware-intrinsic features 
rather than overfitting to modulation-dependent 
statistics [19]–[22].  
Domain-informed 
augmentations, 
particularly modeling channel effects (~41%) and 
hardware impairments (~31%), are critical for 
robustness, as confirmed in subfigure 8(d) [23],

In summary, RF-SSL demonstrates that 
semi-supervised 
consistency 
regularization, 
when 
combined 
with 
domain-informed 
augmentation, multi-task pretraining, and CNN 
inductive 
biases, 
substantially 
enhances 
convergence, temporal stability, modulation 
generalization, and open-set robustness in 
extreme few-shot RF fingerprinting scenarios, 
establishing a practical framework for real-
world, resource-constrained IoT, UAV, and 
tactical deployments [19]–[26].  
 
Limitations  
 
RF-SSL demonstrates promise but faces notable 
limitations. Absolute performance is modest: 
few-shot accuracy rarely exceeds 0.90, zero-shot 
anomaly AUC stays below 0.90, and severe 
SNR, temporal drift, or channel impairments 
drop accuracy below 0.20, reflecting the 
challenge of extracting reliable hardware 
fingerprints from limited data in open-set, noisy 
RF environments [19], [20]. It is highly 
sensitive 
to 
hyperparameters, 
incurs 
computational overhead from DIA and multi-
task pretraining, lacks extensive real-world 
validation, and does not yet support online 
adaptation or continual learning [21]–[24].  
 
Future Directions  
 
Future work on RF-SSL should prioritize 
several key advancements. First, integrate 
physics-informed 
generative 
models 
(e.g., 
diffusion or flow-based) to synthesize realistic 
impairment trajectories and device ageing 
patterns, reducing reliance on hand-crafted 
augmentations and improving robustness under 
unseen 
distortions 
[25]. 
Second, 
develop 
adaptive 
hyperparameter 
optimization 
frameworks, such as Bayesian optimization or 
meta-learning-based tuning, to automate the 
search for optimal temperature, learning rate, 
and batch size across new datasets or hardware 
types [26]. Third, explore continual/semi-
supervised lifelong learning mechanisms that 
enable online model updates from unlabeled 
field data while preserving knowledge of 
previously seen devices and modulations [20]. 
Fourth, 
conduct 
large-scale 
real-world 
evaluations on heterogeneous IoT/UAV/tactical 
networks spanning multiple frequency bands, 
protocols, and environmental conditions to 
validate generalization beyond simulations [23]. 
Finally, hybridize RF-SSL with emerging 
lightweight architectures (e.g., efficient CNN-
Transformer hybrids or spiking neural networks) 
to further reduce inference latency and power 
consumption for edge deployment, targeting 
>0.8 accuracy under practical constraints while 
maintaining 
the 
demonstrated 
robustness 
advantages [22], [24].

CONCLUSION 
 
The comprehensive experimental evaluation of 
RF-SSL demonstrates that semi-supervised 
learning, when augmented with carefully 
designed domain-informed strategies, offers 
meaningful advantages for few-shot device 
identification and zero-shot anomaly detection 
in 
challenging 
RF 
environments. 
Across 
multiple 
regimes—few-shot 
labeled 
data 
scarcity (1–20 shots), zero-shot rogue/spoofing 
detection, SNR/channel impairment variations, 
temporal drift over one year, unseen modulation 
schemes, and severe operational distortions—
RF-SSL 
consistently 
outperforms 
purely 
supervised baselines in robustness, convergence 
speed (~3× faster), and relative performance 
retention. Key enablers include the domain-
informed 
augmentation 
(DIA) 
module 
(providing 
+15–20% 
gains), 
multi-
task/contrastive pretraining (yielding the richest 
representations), 
shallow-to-medium 
CNN-
dominant architectures (best speed-accuracy-
robustness 
trade-off), 
and 
precise 
hyperparameter 
tuning 
(especially 
low 
contrastive temperature τ ≈ 0.1 and LR = 1e-3). 
Ablation studies confirm additive contributions 
from each component, with DIA and contrastive 
pretext driving the largest improvements, while 
interactions remain largely synergistic within 
optimal ranges.  
Nevertheless, 
absolute 
performance 
remains constrained: few-shot accuracies rarely 
exceed 0.90, anomaly AUC stays below 0.90, 
and severe impairment regimes yield accuracies 
<0.20, underscoring the fundamental difficulty 
of reliably extracting stable, device-specific 
hardware fingerprints from limited, noisy, non-
stationary RF signals in open-set conditions. 
Despite these limitations, RF-SSL achieves 
practical headroom, modest but consistent gains 
in data efficiency, convergence, long-term 
stability, 
and 
cross-domain 
generalization, 
making it a promising foundation for resource-
constrained, 
dynamic-spectrum 
applications 
such as IoT security, UAV identification, and 
tactical emitter tracking.

Zigbee is a popular communication protocol in the Internet of things (IoT) which shows great potential
in smart home. However, the smart device has the risk of being hijacked by unauthorized users and
may result in privacy disclosure. Traditional device identification is based on cryptography which is
easy to be cracked. Recently, radio frequency fingerprinting identification (RFFID) is popular in device
identification. Traditional RFFID’s power consumption and cost is unacceptable to Zigbee. In order

1. Introduction
With the development of communication technique, IoT
makes our life become smarter and more convenient. However,
smart device also causes privacy disclosure. Traditional IoT iden-
tification is based on cryptography. It uses complex algorithms to
encrypt the Identification code. This method is easy to be cracked
by hostile people [1,2]. Once the hacker succeeds, they can add
a variety of malicious software in the device to achieve data
interception and theft. It may cause terrible result, and limit the
implementation of Zigbee. This crisis has led to the development
of identification technology using radio frequency fingerprinting
(RFF) in the physical layer. RFF is a feature that can represent
a device steadily and separately. Thus, it can be thought as the
DNA of device. RFF appears as carrier frequency offset (CFO), In-
phase (I) and Quadrature (Q) offset, non-linear variation. It is
based on the minor difference of transmitting device [3]. Even
the same batch of products from the same manufacturer will be
different [4]. It is hard to collect the RFF features, although the
RFF has great benefits.
Tradition radio frequency fingerprinting identification (RFFID)
methods are usually based on support vector machine (SVM) or
decision tree (DT), random forest (RF) which are the classical
machine learning methods. Restricted by the performance of
the machine learning methods mentioned above, the dataset for
training needs complex pre-processing [5–7]. In order to reduce

In 2003, Hall et al. from Canada proposed for the first time in
literature [9] that individual identification of Bluetooth devices
could be achieved by extracting subtle differences in Bluetooth
signals, and defined such subtle features as ‘‘RF fingerprint’’.
In 2005, Ureten, O. et al. in literature [10] divided RFID into
three stages: transient detection, feature extraction and finger-
print classification. In 2006, Barbuau, M. et al. introduced in
the literature [11] an intrusion detection system against man-
in-the-middle attacks using RF fingerprint identification technol-
ogy. In 2007, Ureten, O. et al. in literature [12] divided RFID
into four steps: pretreatment, detection, feature extraction and
classification, and introduced a complete Wi-Fi RF fingerprint
identification system. In 2008, Suski, W.C. et al. divided RFID fin-
gerprint recognition into four steps in literature [13]: waveform
parameter extraction, transient detection, feature extraction and
classification of unknown received signals, and proposed to carry
out individual identification of three IEEE802.11a communication
devices based on OFDM signal spectrum characteristics. In 2009,
Danev, B. et al. identified the node through the transient char-
acteristics of RF signals emitted by the wireless sensor node in
literature [14]. In 2009, Klein, R. W. et al. proposed in litera-
ture [15] that RF fingerprint identification is one of the physical

published in 2008. The experimental results show that the correct
recognition rate of seven UMTS user devices with different mod-

same models, the correct recognition rate is 85%. For recognition,

in 2008, the use of more than 130 wireless card for experiment,
and points out that the wireless network card equipment in the
difference exists in the process of producing process, can extract
signal wireless network frame, and map it to the modulation
domain, the related features of these differences can be shown,
and then design a passive radio frequency identification system
equipment, and use of machine learning algorithms to realize
the function, the experimental results show that the correct
recognition rate of IEEE 802.11b devices used in experiments can
reach 99%. In 2014, Peng et al. argued in literature [19] that in
the field of relay authentication and recognition of collaborative
relay systems, the I/Q imbalance of modulation domain could
be used as a RF fingerprint of a device. This idea is verified
by numerical simulation based on the authentication of two-
parameter hypothesis test and likelihood ratio test. Finally, the
simulation results prove the correctness of the idea, and the
authentication performance of the system is improved obviously.
In 2015, aiming at the classification problem of IEEE 802.15.4
2.4 GHz RF equipment in Si Labs, Knox et al. collected and
demodulated signals from five devices of this type from the
same manufacturer in literature [20], and took Ettus Labs USPR1
software radio platform as the receiving device with a sampling
rate of 4M. The phase information of baseband signal is extracted
after filtering and noise reduction and used as RF fingerprint. The
experimental results show that the classification performance
of the RF fingerprint varies with temperature difference and
channel distance difference. The shorter the channel distance, the
higher the average classification accuracy. For the identification
of RFID devices and e-passports, Danev et al. proposed a variety
of fingerprint extraction methods in literature [21] and further
classification and identification by using the nearest neighbor
algorithm and SVM method. Experimental results showed that
the final false positives rate was less than 5%, proving the ef-
fectiveness of this method. According to the existing literature,
since the hardware information of the communication equipment
transmitter is more stored in the steady state signal, the finger-
print characteristics of the stead state signal can be analyzed to
achieve better recognition performance.

3.1. Structure of lightweight CNN
CNN is a classical model in the area of image identification,
it also shows wonderful performance in feature extraction. CNN
usually consist of convolution layers, pooling layers, dense layers.
The detail descriptions of those layers are as follow:
Convolution layer: This layer is used to extract the feature
of the dataset which can replace the role of data pre-process in
most cases. By using the convolution kernel, the neural network
reduces the dimension of input data with the valuable feature
collected. Thus, with the help of convolution layer, many complex
data-processing can be avoided.
Pooling layer: Pooling layer also named down-sampling layer.
It usually be used to reduce the number of parameters. Max
pooling and average pooling are common methods of pooling.
However, pooling layers will also reduce the accuracy of neural
networks.
Dense layer: Dense layer is used to map the feature space to
sample space, which is necessary in classification model. How-
ever, before the features be send into the Dense layer, they
must be flattened. This results in the increase of parameters and
training times.

5. Conclusion
This paper proposed a lightweight CNN to identify Zigbee
devices and compare it with the common CNN and classical ma-
chine learning methods. Both of them has excellent performance
in high SNR environment. The simulation result shows that the
performance of lightweight CNN proposed is better than the ma-
chine learning methods, such as SVM, DT, the performance of it
is worse than the common CNN. However, the cost of lightweight
CNN proposed is much smaller than the common CNN.

Abstract
We present a novel technique for radio transmitter iden-
tiﬁcation based on frequency domain characteristics. Our
technique detects the unique features imbued in a signal
as it passes through a transmit chain.
We are the ﬁrst
to propose the use of discriminatory classiﬁers based on
steady state spectral features. In laboratory experiments,
we achieve 97% accuracy at 30dB SNR and 66% accuracy
at 0dB SNR based on eight identical Universal Software Ra-
dio Peripherals (USRP) transmitters. Our technique can be
implemented using today’s low cost high-volume receivers
and requires no manual performance tuning.
1. Introduction
In this paper we describe a new technique for identify-
ing a radio transmitter via RF ﬁngerprinting. Our technique
exploits the aggregate effect of differences introduced dur-
ing transmitter manufacturer. Differences in component de-
sign (ﬁlters, power ampliﬁers, inductors, capacitors), same
component manufacturing tolerance spread, PCB materials
and PCB soldering etc. These differences are imbued in
the transmitted signal the and effect can be detected at the
receiver. Our method assumes the receiver’s frequency re-
sponse remains constant. The only differences in the digital
baseband samples produced by the receiver’s radio are due
to different transmitters and noise and interference.
Identiﬁcation of a radio transmitter at the physical layer
would enjoy many applications. Gerdes et al.[2] give a di-
verse list of possibilities; intrusion detection, authentica-
tion, forensic data collection and defect detection monitor-
ing. Our work was motivated by a cellular wireless applica-
tion of femto base stations[5]. This application is a special
case of authentication. It involves reducing the core net-
work signaling load due to location management in GSM
and UMTS cellular networks. As cells reduce in size, it
often desirable to limit cell access to only a subset of an
operator’s subscriber base. For example, an end customer
may install a femto base station and expect exclusive access
to it. That is, other mobile phones on the same network
may sense the femto cell but when they attempt to camp on
it they are to be denied access. From a logical view point
denying access is straightforward. The temporary ID pro-
vided by the handset is mapped to an absolute ID via signal-
ing to the core network. Based on this absolute ID the femto
either permits or denies access. However the large increase
in cells and resulting large increase in location area updates
means the core network experiences a very large increase
in signaling. If we can identify a mobile phone at ﬁrst con-
tact with the basestation using RF ﬁngerprinting, we can
provide an elegant solution to the challenge of suppressing
signaling trafﬁc at higher layers.
The rest of the paper is organised as follows. In Section 2
we review the previous work described in the literature. In
Section 3 we describe our proposed approach and in Sec-
tion 4 we describe our experimental setup and how we cap-
ture the data for testing our approach. Finally, we present
the results in Section 5 and conclude in Section 6.
2. Background and Previous Work
Several researchers have reported the possibility of iden-
tifying a radio transmitter by analysing the received sig-
nals. This work stretches back to 1940s and radar trans-
mitter identiﬁcation [6]. The majority of techniques focus
on transmissions at the physical layer.
Physical layer ﬁngerprinting techniques may be split into
two groups: transient signal techniques and steady state
